hero_heading: Henderson Caps How Many Junk Cars You Can Keep
hero_description: The number is six, four, or two depending on your zoning — not one flat figure across the city. Work out which applies to you, then decide what to do about it.

sections.heading: Six, Four, or Two — It Depends Where You Live
paragraphs: Henderson's property maintenance code limits how many inoperable or unregistered vehicles a property may keep, and the limit is tied to the property's zoning designation rather than applied as one flat figure across the city. Properties in an RNP-1 designated area are allowed up to six. RNP-2 areas are allowed up to four. Every other property is limited to two.

That makes the first useful question not whether anyone has complained, but which of those three categories your address falls into. It is the fact that decides whether you are comfortably inside the limit or already over it, and it is knowable before anyone knocks on your door.

Worth knowing too: Henderson is an incorporated city and enforces its own property maintenance and nuisance code through its own code enforcement office, separately from Clark County. Advice written for the unincorporated valley does not necessarily describe what applies at a Henderson address.

image.alt: An older sedan parked on the driveway of a single-storey suburban home

sections.heading: The Fence Rule, and the 72-Hour Exception
paragraphs: Two conditions sit alongside the count, and both are narrower than people usually assume.

Where Henderson allows inoperable or unregistered vehicles to be kept, they must be screened by a substantially opaque fence at least six feet high. Read that carefully: screening is a requirement placed on vehicles that are already within the permitted number. Building a fence does not buy you an extra vehicle.

Separately, Henderson allows a single inoperable vehicle that is registered to a resident of the property and undergoing minor repair work, for a period not exceeding 72 hours. Both halves of that matter. It covers a car registered to someone who lives there, being actively worked on, for three days — not a vehicle that has sat untouched since last spring.

sections.heading: Bring It Into Line, or Let It Go
paragraphs: If the count at your address is over the limit, there are only two directions to go: bring the property into compliance, or reduce the number of vehicles. A six-foot opaque fence is a real project. Selling the one that has not run in years is usually the shorter road, and it is the only one that also clears the space.
If you are inside the limit and simply tired of looking at it, none of the above applies and the decision is entirely yours. We buy vehicles running or not, damaged or complete, either way.

faq.question: How do I find out whether my property is RNP-1, RNP-2, or neither?
faq.answer: It is your property's zoning designation, and it is the fact the whole limit turns on. Henderson enforces its own code through its own code enforcement office, so the city is the place to confirm it rather than a county source.

faq.question: If I put up a fence, can I keep an extra vehicle?
faq.answer: No. Screening by a substantially opaque fence at least six feet high is a condition placed on vehicles that are already within the permitted number. It is not a way to exceed the count.

faq.question: My car is mid-repair. Does the 72-hour allowance cover me?
faq.answer: Only if it is registered to someone living at the property and the work is minor repair, and only for a period not exceeding 72 hours. A vehicle that has been sitting for months is not what that allowance describes.

faq.question: Do the same rules apply just outside the city?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Henderson is incorporated and enforces its own property maintenance and nuisance code separately from Clark County, so a neighbouring unincorporated address is not governed by the figures on this page.
